questions.q: What is service discovery, as this lesson defines it?
options: A Docker Hub feature for finding public images
The ability for one container to find another by a stable name instead of a hardcoded, changeable IP address
A monitoring tool that lists every running container
A command that automatically restarts failed containers
questions.explain: Service discovery here means containers resolving each other by name -- the same embedded-DNS mechanism from Lesson 21, applied to a real application connection.

options: A hardcoded IP address that must be updated manually if the database container is recreated
The `checkout-db` container's name as the hostname, resolved automatically by Docker's embedded DNS
A file path on the host machine
The Docker Hub repository where the checkout-db image is stored
questions.explain: The hostname in that connection string is checkout-db -- the container's name, not an IP. This is exactly what lets the database be recreated freely without breaking the app's configuration.

questions.q: What must be true for `checkout` to actually be able to resolve `checkout-db` by name?
options: Nothing extra is required -- all containers can resolve each other by name by default
Both containers must be running the exact same image
Both containers must be attached to the same user-defined network
`checkout-db` must be started with the `--mount` flag instead of `-v`
questions.explain: Name resolution only works because both checkout and checkout-db are started with --network northbridge-checkout-net -- the shared user-defined network is what enables it.

questions.q: What does `docker logs checkout` showing `Connected to checkout-db:5432` confirm?
options: That checkout-db has exceeded its storage limit
That the checkout application successfully resolved checkout-db's name to its current IP and connected
That checkout and checkout-db are running inside the same container
That the connection failed and fell back to a default address
questions.explain: That log line is the proof the pattern worked -- the app asked for checkout-db by name, Docker's embedded DNS resolved it, and the connection succeeded.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the catalog/catalog-db and checkout/checkout-db setups as using the same underlying pattern?
options: Because they share the exact same user-defined network
Because both pair a named volume for persistence with a user-defined network for name-based discovery -- just scoped to each service's own containers
Because catalog and checkout are actually the same application under different names
Because both use the `host` network driver instead of `bridge`
questions.explain: Each service gets its own volume, its own user-defined network, and a config pointing at its database by container name -- the same reusable pattern applied twice, on two separate networks.
